newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 30-, 15-yr mortgage rates fall in week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. 30-, 15-yr mortgage rates fall in week.

text.p: Average commitment rates on U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgages fell to 8.28 percent in the week ended September 13 from 8.34 percent the previous week, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp said Thursday.
Fifteen-year mortgages also fell to an average 7.81 percent from 7.88 percent last week, Freddie Mac said.
But one-year adjustable-rate mortgages inched up to an average 5.90 percent from 5.85 percent last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.60 percent, the 15-year 7.12 percent, and the ARM 5.80 percent.
"This week's figures reflect an element of stability in the bond market after fears of inflation caused interest rates to rise last week," Freddie Mac Chief Economist Robert Van Order said.

"Recent news that housing prices have risen at an annualized rate of 4.1 percent nationally coupled with interest rates in the affordable eight to 8.5 percent range makes homeownership even more attractive, which should translate into a good year for home sales," Van Order added.
On Friday, the Labor Department will issue U.S. August consumer prices. Earlier this month Labor reported August unemployment at 5.1 percent, the lowest since March 1989.

The Federal Reserve said Wednesday in its Beige Book that there was no clear-cut evidence of mounting inflation in August although signs of wage pressures exist. But some economists expect the Federal Open Market Committee to raise interest rates when it meets September 24.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans and 1.4 percent on ARM loans, both unchanged from last week. They charged 1.7 percent on 15-year mortgages, up from 1.6 percent last week.
